## Background

Human capital theory treats education as an investment. A year of
school costs tuition and the earnings you give up while you study, and
it pays off in higher earnings for the rest of your working life. In
class we measured the payoff with the **human capital earnings
function**:

$$
\ln I = \alpha + rS + \beta_1 EXP + \beta_2 EXP^2 + \varepsilon
$$

Here $I$ is earnings, $S$ is years of schooling, and $EXP$ is potential
experience, the number of years since the person left school. When the
direct costs of schooling are small, the coefficient $r$ is the return
to schooling: the approximate percentage increase in earnings from one
more year of school. The textbook's Table 14.2 estimates this equation
with data from Statistics Canada's Canadian Income Survey for 2022. It
finds a return of 10.3% for men and 15.2% for women.

In this assignment you will use the public use microdata file of the
same survey. You will draw age-earnings profiles, estimate the human
capital earnings function for men and for women, and see how leaving a
variable out of the regression biases the estimate of $r$. That is the
problem behind ability bias.

## The data

The data come from the public use microdata file of Statistics Canada's
Canadian Income Survey (CIS) for 2022. Each row is one person aged 25 to
64: 38,367 people in all. The file keeps 8 of the survey's variables,
with Statistics Canada's own names and codes. Income is for the 2022
calendar year.

Read these notes before you start.

-   **No weights.** The survey sampled some kinds of people more
    heavily than others, and Statistics Canada provides weights to
    correct for that. To keep things simple, this file leaves the
    weights out, and you will treat every person the same. Your results
    will show the same patterns as the textbook's, but your numbers will
    differ a little from its Table 14.2.
-   **Employees only.** `ALHRWK` counts hours at all jobs, including
    self-employment, so for a self-employed person `WGSAL / ALHRWK`
    would not be an hourly wage. The file therefore leaves out everyone
    with income from self-employment. It also leaves out people who
    report wages but no hours of work, and people whose immigrant status
    is not known.
-   **Broad categories.** To protect the people in the survey, the
    public file records age in five-year groups and education in four
    broad levels, and it rounds income amounts.

| Variable | Description |
|:-----------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| `PERSONID` | Person identifier |
| `PROV` | Province: 10 Newfoundland and Labrador, 11 Prince Edward Island, 12 Nova Scotia, 13 New Brunswick, 24 Quebec, 35 Ontario, 46 Manitoba, 47 Saskatchewan, 48 Alberta, 59 British Columbia |
| `AGEGP` | Age group: 6 25 to 29, 7 30 to 34, 8 35 to 39, 9 40 to 44, 10 45 to 49, 11 50 to 54, 12 55 to 59, 13 60 to 64 |
| `SEX` | 1 male, 2 female |
| `HLEV2G` | Highest level of education: 1 less than high school, 2 high school graduate, 3 postsecondary certificate or diploma below a university degree, 4 university degree, 9 not stated |
| `IMMST` | Immigrant status: 1 immigrant, 2 non-immigrant |
| `WGSAL` | Wages and salaries in 2022, before taxes and deductions, in dollars. 0 for people with no wages |
| `ALHRWK` | Hours worked in 2022, at all jobs. 9996 for people who did not work |

Source: Adapted from Statistics Canada, Canadian Income Survey, 2022,
Public Use Microdata File (catalogue 72M0003X). This does not
constitute an endorsement by Statistics Canada of this product.

## Question 3: Leaving a Variable Out

In class we saw that if log earnings depend on schooling and ability
$A$,

$$
\ln I = \alpha + \beta S + \gamma A + \varepsilon,
$$

and ability is related to schooling, $A = \delta_0 + \delta_1 S + v$,
then a regression that leaves $A$ out estimates
$\tilde{\beta} = \beta + \gamma\delta_1$. You cannot check this with
ability, because the survey does not measure it. But the formula holds
for any variable left out of a regression, so you can watch it work
with one that is in the data: immigrant status.

When the regression has other variables in it too, as yours does,
$\gamma$ is the coefficient on the left-out variable in the regression
that includes it, and $\delta_1$ is the coefficient on $S$ in a
regression of the left-out variable on $S$ and the other variables.

**(a)** Add `immigrant` to `men` and to `women`: 1 if `IMMST` is 1, and

-   the **auxiliary regression**: `immigrant` on `S`, `EXP` and `EXP2`.
    Store the results as `men_aux` and `women_aux`.
